title: EUR 140,000 cover arrived from a bank the announcement never named
explain:
An MT103 announced EUR 140,000 and named the correspondent that would send the cover.
The cover arrived from a different bank entirely.
The beneficiary bank could not match the two legs and would not credit the beneficiary.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 announcement states field 53
→ Beneficiary bank knows where funds will come from
→ Cover arrives from an unmentioned bank
→ Beneficiary bank will not credit

The assumption was:
"The cover will arrive from somewhere. The source does not matter."
The announcement must name the cover's source.

Why?

In a cover payment the MT103 announcement should state in field 53 which correspondent will send the cover, so the beneficiary bank knows where the funds will come from. When the cover arrives from a bank the announcement never mentioned, the beneficiary bank cannot match the two legs and will not credit the beneficiary.

The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree.

What proves the cover came from the bank the announcement named?

BA Takeaway

State the cover's source in field 53 of the MT103 announcement. If the cover arrives from another bank, the sender's bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Cover source in field 53
→ Cover arrives from that bank
→ Two legs match
→ Beneficiary credited

The real requirement isn't "Has the cover arrived?"

It's "What evidence proves the cover came from the bank the announcement named?"

Have you ever held a payment because the cover came from an unmentioned bank?
takeaway: The fix sits with the sender, whose bank must correct the announcement so the two legs agree.

title: EUR 50,000 pacs.008 rejected, and the pacs.002 was booked as a payment
explain:
A EUR 50,000 pacs.008 was rejected.
The pacs.002 that reported it was booked as a debit.
The same payment was counted twice, and the books no longer balanced.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 sent for EUR 50,000
→ Payment rejected, pacs.002 reports it
→ pacs.002 booked as a debit
→ Same payment counted twice

The assumption was:
"Every message that arrives gets a posting."
A pacs.002 reports an outcome. It moves no money.

Why?

A pacs.002 reports the outcome of a pacs.008; it moves no money, so it normally needs no accounting entry of its own. When it carries a negative acknowledgement, the postings made for the original payment are undone exactly, debit and credit reversed, restoring the books to their pre-payment position.

Booking the status report itself as a debit or credit would count the same payment twice.

What proves the books were restored, not double-counted?

BA Takeaway

Book nothing for the pacs.002 itself. On a negative acknowledgement, reverse the original postings exactly, debit and credit, and check the books are back to their pre-payment position.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Original postings
→ Exact reversal
→ Books restored
→ No posting for the report

The real requirement isn't "Should we book the pacs.002?"

It's "What evidence proves the books were restored, not double-counted?"

Have you ever seen a status report booked as if it were a payment?
takeaway: Booking the status report itself as a debit or credit would count the same payment twice.

title: The nostro showed EUR 1 million. The mirror showed something else.
explain:
A EUR 1 million credit lands on the nostro.
The mirror account still shows the old balance.
Treasury funds the day on a balance that is already wrong.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 1 million credited to the nostro
→ Correspondent advises with MT910 or MT950
→ Mirror updated late, from a daily batch
→ Treasury works on a stale mirror balance

The requirement said:
"The mirror nostro updates once a day, in a batch."

Why?

Every movement on the real nostro is mirrored one transaction at a time, never in a daily batch. When the nostro is credited, the correspondent advises the holder, for example with an MT910 or MT950, and the mirror is updated from that advice. When the bank instructs its correspondent to debit the nostro, the mirror is updated at once, and the two entries always carry the same amount with opposite signs.

Mirror nostro moves transaction by transaction, never in a batch.

BA Takeaway

Update the mirror from each advice as it arrives, and never let a batch stand between the nostro and the mirror.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Real nostro movements
→ Correspondent advice
→ Mirror updates

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the mirror matches the real nostro right now?"

Have you funded a day on a mirror balance that was already out of date?
takeaway: Mirror nostro moves transaction by transaction, never in a batch.

title: A debit on the nostro, a credit on the mirror, and a team that read it backwards.
explain:
A EUR 300,000 debit hits the nostro.
The mirror shows a credit of EUR 300,000.
The team reports a gain, and treasury releases funds that were never there.

Here is how that happens:

→ EUR 300,000 debit on the real nostro
→ Mirror shows a EUR 300,000 credit
→ Team reads the mirror as a gain
→ Funds released against money that left

The requirement said:
"A credit on the mirror means money arrived."

Why?

A debit on the real nostro appears as a credit on the mirror, and a credit on the real account appears as a debit on the mirror, always for the same amount. The mirror reflects the real account, so the two sides sit opposite by design rather than by coincidence. Reading the mirror balance and its movements therefore tells a bank exactly what the real account should show.

Mirror nostro always shows the opposite sign, by design.

BA Takeaway

Read every mirror entry with its sign flipped, and reconcile the mirror against the real account before acting on it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Real nostro entry
→ Mirror entry
→ Sign convention

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves this mirror entry means money in, not money out?"

Have you seen a mirror balance read backwards?
takeaway: Mirror nostro always shows the opposite sign, by design.

title: Small breaks, ignored for months, added up to a USD 2 million surprise before the audit.
explain:
Small uncleared items pile up for months, each one looking harmless.
Volumes rise, and a USD 2 million discrepancy appears just before an audit.
The team had optimised the manual workaround, never the process that created the breaks.

Here is how that happens:

→ Small breaks accumulate for months
→ Two systems derive value dates differently
→ USD 2 million discrepancy found before the audit
→ Manual workaround optimised, root cause untouched

The requirement said:
"Small breaks are harmless until the audit."

Why?

Small uncleared items accumulated for months, looking harmless, until rising volumes exposed a 2 million dollar discrepancy just before an audit. The cause was timing: two systems derived the transaction value date with different logic. Aligning that logic cleared 80 percent of breaks automatically, which is the lesson to keep: fix the process that creates the break, never optimise the manual workaround, and run reconciliation as an early-warning system.

Fix the process that creates the break, not the workaround.

BA Takeaway

Align the logic that creates breaks, and run reconciliation as an early warning, not as a month-end chore.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Value date logic
→ Break aging
→ Reconciliation alerts

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves the process that creates these breaks is fixed?"

Have you optimised a workaround while the break kept coming back?
takeaway: Fix the process that creates the break, not the workaround.

title: One empty parameter passed QA, staging and a small rollout. At full volume it broke everything.
explain:
A new flow passes QA, staging and a small rollout.
At full volume a parameter everyone assumed was always filled comes back empty.
Partner API calls fail, reconciliation mismatches, and the fix takes three hours while trust takes far longer to rebuild.

Here is how that happens:

→ Small rollout goes clean
→ Full volume exposes an empty parameter
→ Partner API calls fail
→ Reconciliation mismatches across the board

The requirement said:
"A parameter that is always filled in testing will always be filled."

Why?

One unchecked assumption can survive QA, staging and a small rollout, then fail at full volume: a parameter assumed to always return a value sometimes came back empty. Partner API calls failed, reconciliation mismatched, and rebuilding partner trust took longer than the three-hour fix. Validate every input, above all the ones assumed always present, and add contract tests with the partner covering empty and null variants of every field.

The parameter everyone assumed was filled is the one that breaks you.

BA Takeaway

Validate every input, above all the ones assumed always present, and test empty and null variants with the partner.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Assumed inputs
→ Contract tests
→ Empty and null variants

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves every assumed input was tested empty and null?"

Have you shipped an assumption that only full volume could expose?
takeaway: The parameter everyone assumed was filled is the one that breaks you.

title: The bank moved its cut-off. The fintech kept sending on the old one, and every payment settled late.
explain:
A bank moves its transaction cut-off time and tells no one.
The fintech keeps sending on the old settlement window.
Requests are accepted, then processed in a later cycle, with green dashboards and no errors anywhere.

Here is how that happens:

→ Bank moves its cut-off time
→ Fintech keeps the old settlement window
→ Requests accepted, settled a cycle late
→ Dashboards stay green, no errors raised

The requirement said:
"If the code is right and the dashboards are green, the payments are fine."

Why?

Code can be perfect and dashboards green while transactions fail, because the bank moved its transaction cut-off time and the fintech kept sending on the old settlement window. Requests were accepted, then processed in a later cycle, breaking user expectations without a single error. Most production incidents in finance are coordination failures of this kind, cut-off changes, holiday calendars, or report timings that moved without notice, so keep cut-off and calendar configuration synced with every bank partner.

Most incidents are coordination failures, not bugs.

BA Takeaway

Sync cut-off and calendar configuration with every bank partner, and treat a partner change as a release, not a rumour.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Partner cut-off times
→ Holiday calendars
→ Configuration sync

The real requirement is not "When do we act?"

It is "What evidence proves your cut-off times match your partners' cut-off times today?"

Have you debugged code for a failure that was really a moved cut-off?
takeaway: Most incidents are coordination failures, not bugs.

title: A EUR 45,000 payment carried rich remittance data, and the last bank in the chain threw it away
explain:
A EUR 45,000 payment was sent with structured purpose and remittance data.

The data was meant to help compliance screening and let the beneficiary reconcile against the right invoice.

The last bank in the chain dropped it, and the beneficiary could not match the payment.

Here's how it happened:

→ Payment sent with structured purpose and remittance data
→ First bank captures it correctly
→ Second bank maps it inconsistently
→ Last bank in the chain drops it, its system cannot consume it
→ Beneficiary cannot reconcile against the right invoice

The assumption was:
"Rich data helps by itself."

Why?

Structured purpose and remittance data helps compliance screening and lets the beneficiary reconcile the payment against the right invoice. But the data is only useful if it is captured correctly, mapped consistently, and consumed by the downstream systems that need it. Poor data quality in one system becomes a compliance and reconciliation problem in the next.

Data that does not survive the chain helps no one.

BA Takeaway

Data quality has to be owned end to end. Name the owner at each hop: who captures, who maps, who consumes, and what happens when a system cannot consume it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Capture, correctly
→ Mapping, consistently
→ Consumption downstream
→ The owner at each hop

The real requirement isn't "Did we send rich data?"

It's "What evidence proves the data survived every hop to the beneficiary?"

Have you seen rich payment data dropped by the last bank in the chain?
takeaway: Data that does not survive the chain helps no one.

title: SAR 250,000 left the account, the beneficiary was paid, and the nostro showed nothing
explain:
A SAR 250,000 payment left the customer account and was sent onward.

The beneficiary was credited.

But the statement showed no nostro debit, and Operations wanted to send the payment again.

Here's how it happened:

→ SAR 250,000 debited from the customer account
→ Payment sent onward to the correspondent
→ Beneficiary credited
→ Corresponding nostro debit never posts
→ Statement shows no debit, team proposes re-effecting the payment

The assumption was:
"No nostro debit means the payment never went."

Why?

This is a Payment Missing a Nostro Entry. The payment left and the beneficiary may already stand credited, but the nostro debit never posted. Re-effecting would duplicate the payment and break the nostro at reconciliation. The governing discipline is evidence before action.

A missing entry is not a missing payment.

BA Takeaway

Prove the payment state first with pacs.002, camt.052 or camt.053, or pacs.028 where no notification arrived. Once proved, the correspondent bank posts the nostro debit. Never re-effect the payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The customer debit
→ The payment state, proved with evidence
→ The nostro debit, posted by the correspondent
→ The re-effecting, forbidden

The real requirement isn't "Did the nostro debit post?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment's state before we touch the nostro?"

Have you seen a payment nearly sent twice because the nostro entry was missing?
takeaway: A missing entry is not a missing payment.

title: A USD 10 million payment was two days late, and the interest bill proved the value date mattered more than the booking
explain:
A USD 10 million payment was delayed by two days.

It was booked on the day it was processed.

The interest bill arrived anyway, because interest runs from the value date, not the booking date.

Here's how it happened:

→ USD 10 million payment processed, booked on the processing day
→ Value date differs from the booking date by two days
→ Customer leg credited on Monday at a Monday value date
→ Nostro leg booked later at that same value date
→ Interest charged on the value date gap, no one had checked it

The assumption was:
"The booking date decides the interest."

Why?

Back valuation is a mismatch between value date and booking date, and it matters because interest runs from the value date, not the booking date. In a single-sided case the mismatch sits on one side, while in a double-sided case it sits on both sides. The working sequence is to confirm the value date first, establish whether the mismatch is single or double-sided, then assess the impact on interest, liquidity and reconciliation.

Value date drives interest, not booking.

BA Takeaway

When a payment is delayed or rebooked, confirm the value date first, then whether the mismatch is single or double-sided, then the impact on interest, liquidity and reconciliation. The booking date is the record. The value date is the money.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The value date
→ The booking date
→ Single-sided or double-sided mismatch
→ The impact on interest, liquidity and reconciliation

The real requirement isn't "When was the payment booked?"

It's "What evidence proves the value date, and what interest does it carry?"

Have you seen an interest bill arrive because no one checked the value date?
takeaway: Value date drives interest, not booking.

title: One settlement code was mapped wrong, and a EUR 150,000 payment was debited twice
explain:
A EUR 150,000 payment arrived with the settlement code INGA.

The migration mapped it as INDA.

The sending bank account was debited again, and the double posting was found at day-end as a reconciliation break.

Here's how it happened:

→ pacs.008 arrives with INGA, the instructing agent has already settled this leg
→ Migration maps INGA as INDA
→ Engine follows INDA logic, the instructed agent settles this leg
→ Sending bank account debited again, a double posting
→ Reconciliation break found at day-end

The assumption was:
"MT to MX migration is a one-to-one field replacement."

Why?

It is not. The settlement method code on a pacs.008 changes the accounting: INDA means the instructed agent settles this leg, while INGA means the instructing agent has already settled it. Information once implied is now explicit and carries business meaning, so an incoming INGA payment wrongly mapped as INDA makes the engine follow the wrong settlement logic.

A code is a business decision, not a field.

BA Takeaway

Migration must ask who settles each leg, whether settlement has already happened, and what accounting entries should follow. A field mapping shows where data goes. Business analysis shows what it means.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The settlement code as sent
→ Who settles this leg
→ Whether settlement already happened
→ The accounting entries that must follow

The real requirement isn't "Where does the field map to?"

It's "What evidence proves the mapped code means the same thing in the new message?"

Have you seen a field mapped right and a meaning mapped wrong?
takeaway: A code is a business decision, not a field.

title: The app said a EUR 850 payment failed, but the account was debited anyway
explain:
A customer sent EUR 850 through a mobile app.

The app showed the payment as failed.

Yet the account statement showed the EUR 850 debit, and the customer asked for the money back.

Here's how it happened:

→ Customer sends EUR 850 through the mobile app
→ App shows the payment as failed
→ Account statement shows the EUR 850 debit
→ Payment is in an uncertain state: the debit may mean it reached clearing and is still processing, or the ledger posted while the payment status update failed
→ Customer asks to retry the payment

The assumption was:
"Failed on screen means failed everywhere."

Why?

It does not. The debit may mean the payment reached the clearing system and is still processing, or it may mean the ledger posted while the payment status update failed. Treat the payment as one transaction with one identity across every system, and use the original instruction ID, end-to-end ID and ledger posting reference to trace it through the channel, the payment engine, the clearing adapter and the core ledger.

One payment, one identity, every system.

BA Takeaway

Do not retry until the true status is known, because a blind retry could create a duplicate payment of EUR 850. Trace the single identity through every system first, then act on what the evidence says.

Keep these controls separate:

→ The app status, failed
→ The ledger posting, debited
→ The true payment status, traced by identity
→ The retry, only after the status is known

The real requirement isn't "Did the app say it failed?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment's true status across every system?"

Have you seen a failed screen hide a payment that actually went through?
takeaway: Do not retry until the true status is known, because a blind retry could create a duplicate payment of EUR 850.

title: Gateway said success, EUR 40,000 never posted
explain:
A payment gateway returns success for a EUR 40,000 supplier payment.
The channel shows the payment as accepted.
Hours later the supplier has not been paid, and the finance team finds no debit in the core banking ledger.

Here's how that happens:

→ pain.001 instruction submitted through the channel
→ Gateway returns a success response
→ Channel shows the payment as accepted
→ Core banking ledger shows no debit
→ Payment engine still shows the payment as in progress

The requirement said:
"If the gateway says success, the payment is done."

The gateway is authoritative for one thing only: acceptance of the instruction. Posting the debit to the ledger is a separate step, and it failed silently. The engine state agreed with neither side, because it was never reconciled against the ledger.

Gateway success ≠ Ledger posted.

BA Takeaway

Separate the three facts and find the authoritative source for each. The gateway proves acceptance. The ledger proves the debit posted. The engine state must be reconciled against both, and a success response from the gateway never proves the ledger posted.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Gateway acceptance
→ Ledger debit posting
→ Payment engine state

The real requirement isn't "Did the gateway accept it?"

It's "What evidence proves the debit posted?"

Have you chased a payment the channel called successful while the ledger said nothing happened?
takeaway: Gateway success does not prove the ledger posted. Check the posting, never trust the channel message.

title: Screen timed out, EUR 25,000 supplier payment in limbo
explain:
A corporate customer submits a EUR 25,000 supplier payment through the online channel.
The screen spins, then times out.
No confirmation appears and no reference is shown. The payment may have been accepted, executed, or never received.

Here's how that happens:

→ Instruction submitted through the online channel
→ Screen spins and times out
→ No confirmation and no reference shown
→ Payment state is unknown

The assumption was:
"If the screen times out, the payment failed."

A timeout only means the response was lost on the way back. The instruction may already have been accepted and executed downstream, so a retry on the same instruction can create a duplicate payment.

A timeout is not a failure. It is an unknown.

BA Takeaway

Make the timeout path explicit in the product. The channel must show a pending or unknown state, never a success and never a failure, until the outcome is confirmed. The status enquiry uses the original correlation ID and payment reference to ask the payment engine, then the ledger, then the downstream clearing status, in that order, and only then is a retry safe.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Channel display state
→ Payment engine state
→ Ledger posting
→ Downstream clearing status

The real requirement isn't "Did the screen time out?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment did or did not happen?"

Have you ever retried a payment after a timeout and found it had already gone through?
takeaway: A timeout is not a failure. It is an unknown, and a retry is safe only once the outcome is confirmed.

explain:
A bank processed 20,000 transactions in a day.
The morning reconciliation showed 500 transactions unmatched between the ledger and the clearing reports.
A report called it a INR 40 lakh loss before anyone had investigated a single item.

Here is what happened:

→ 20,000 transactions processed
→ Ledger compared with clearing reports
→ 500 transactions unmatched, an unmatched rate of 2.5 percent
→ Illustrative exposure calculated as 500 multiplied by an average of INR 8,000, giving INR 40 lakh
→ The illustrative figure reported as a confirmed loss

The requirement said:
"Report the unmatched exposure as the loss."

So a framing figure became a headline loss, and the real investigation started on the back foot.

Why?

Unmatched is not lost. Most unmatched items turn out to be timing differences, late clearing files, or posting lags that resolve on their own. The INR 40 lakh figure frames the scale of the problem, but the real exposure is only known once the unmatched transactions are investigated one by one.

Unmatched is a question, not a loss.

BA Takeaway

Population, unmatched rate and confirmed loss are three different numbers, so keep them separate:

→ 20,000 transactions processed
→ 500 unmatched, 2.5 percent
→ Confirmed loss only after item by item investigation

The real requirement is not "How big is the gap?"

It is "What evidence proves which unmatched items are real losses, and which are timing?"

Have you ever seen an illustrative exposure reported as a confirmed loss?
takeaway: Unmatched is a question, not a loss.

title: App says EUR 4,120, the bank says EUR 3,850
explain:
A customer checks the mobile app and sees a balance of EUR 4,120.
She calls the contact centre, and the agent's screen shows EUR 3,850.
The difference is EUR 270, exactly the amount of a card payment she made that morning.

Here's how that happens:

→ Card payment of EUR 270 made this morning
→ Mobile app shows EUR 4,120
→ Contact centre screen shows EUR 3,850

The assumption was:
"One balance must be wrong."

Neither balance is wrong. The ledger balance is the posted balance in the core banking system and it is authoritative for posted funds, while the app balance may include pending or unposted items. The EUR 270 difference is the pending card payment, so the two balances are both accurate for what they represent, and the fix is to explain the difference rather than to change either balance.

Two balances can both be right. They measure different things.

BA Takeaway

Start by defining what each balance means before touching either one. The ledger balance is posted funds. The app balance may include pending items. When the difference matches a pending payment exactly, the answer is an explanation, not a correction.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Ledger balance, posted funds
→ Available balance
→ Pending and unposted items

The real requirement isn't "Which balance is wrong?"

It's "What evidence proves what each balance represents?"

Have you ever had to explain to a customer why two screens showed two different balances, and both were right?
takeaway: The EUR 270 difference is the pending card payment, so the two balances are both accurate for what they represent.

title: One payment, three different amounts
explain:
A cross-border payment complaint shows one amount in the online banking screen, a different amount transmitted by the API, and a third value held in the database.
The beneficiary address looks complete on screen, but arrives truncated in the payment message.
EUR 8,000 was sent. Nobody can agree what the payment actually says.

Here's how that happens:

→ Customer enters the payment on screen
→ Screen displays one amount and a full address
→ API transmits a different amount
→ Database holds a third value
→ Payment message arrives with a truncated address

The assumption was:
"If the screen looks right, the payment is right."

The value changed somewhere between the screen and the message. Fix the record first: pick one affected payment and its stable identifier, such as the end-to-end identification, and use that single identifier at every layer so the comparison is about the same record. Then capture the value at each point, what the customer entered and what the screen displayed, the API request payload as received, the transformed canonical model, the validation and defaulting applied, and the persisted record, to find where the value changed.

The screen is not the payment. The message is.

BA Takeaway

Trace one payment through every layer with one identifier. The screen, the API payload, the canonical model and the persisted record are four different facts, and the defect sits at the layer where the value first changes.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Value entered and displayed
→ API request payload as received
→ Transformed canonical model
→ Validation and defaulting applied
→ Persisted record

The real requirement isn't "What did the customer type?"

It's "What evidence proves where the value changed between the screen and the message?"

Have you ever traced one payment through five layers and found the value changed in the middle?
takeaway: Capture the value at each point to find where it changed, using one stable identifier at every layer.

title: Migration rehearsal: thousands of mismatches
explain:
A bank migrates from a legacy core system to a new platform.
The first rehearsal shows thousands of mismatches: names that do not match, addresses that cannot be placed into the new structured format, dates in different formats, and payment records whose beneficiary details are incomplete.
Thousands of customers, and the new platform cannot tell who they are.

Here's how that happens:

→ Legacy data extracted
→ Field mapping applied
→ Data transformed and loaded
→ Control totals fail at every stage

The assumption was:
"Move the data, then check it."

A migration without proof at each stage is a hope, not a plan. Define the migration as a controlled data movement with proof at every stage: start with a field-level mapping from the legacy system to the new platform, with every source field, its target field, its transformation rule, its validation rule and its owner, then prove the movement with control totals and exception handling at each stage.

A migration without proof at each stage is a hope, not a plan.

BA Takeaway

Write the field-level mapping before moving a single record, and prove the movement with control totals and exception handling at every stage. A name, an address, a date and a beneficiary record each need a named owner and a validation rule.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Source field and target field
→ Transformation rule
→ Validation rule
→ Control totals per stage
→ Exception handling

The real requirement isn't "Did the data move?"

It's "What evidence proves every field arrived intact at each stage?"

Have you ever watched a rehearsal fail on thousands of records because nobody had mapped the fields first?
takeaway: A migration without proof at each stage is a hope, not a plan.

title: Rs 18,500 debited, the order never arrived
explain:
A customer pays Rs 18,500 for an order through a retailer's checkout.
The bank account is debited, the payment gateway reports success, and the order remains pending.
No confirmation, no dispatch, no delivery date. The money is gone and the goods never move.

Here's how that happens:

→ Customer pays Rs 18,500 at checkout
→ Bank account debited
→ Gateway reports success
→ Order stays pending, no confirmation

The assumption was:
"Gateway success means the order exists."

The payment outcome was lost at one of four boundaries, and the fulfilment path and the refund path depend on which one failed. Start by fixing the reference: take the payment reference from the customer's bank statement and the gateway transaction ID, and confirm they belong to the same payment. Then trace the four boundaries in order, the gateway, the bank, the merchant callback and the order creation, to find where the payment outcome was lost.

A debit without an order is a broken boundary, not a lost payment.

BA Takeaway

Fix the reference first, then trace the four boundaries in order. The gateway, the bank, the merchant callback and the order creation each get checked, because the fix depends on which boundary lost the outcome.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Gateway outcome
→ Bank outcome
→ Merchant callback
→ Order creation

The real requirement isn't "Was the customer charged?"

It's "What evidence proves which boundary lost the payment outcome?"

Have you ever paid for an order, been debited, and watched the order sit pending for days?
takeaway: Trace the four boundaries in order, the gateway, the bank, the merchant callback and the order creation, to find where the payment outcome was lost.

title: Paid and confirmed, but the shop never saw the order
explain:
A retailer runs a checkout where the payment gateway returns a success response.
The customer sees a confirmation screen, and then nothing happens.
The order system never receives the callback, so no order is created, no goods are picked, and the customer is charged for a purchase the retailer cannot see.

Here's how that happens:

→ Gateway returns success
→ Customer sees a confirmation screen
→ Order system never receives the callback
→ No order created, customer charged

The requirement said:
"Show the customer success as soon as the gateway answers."

The outcome was lost between the gateway and the order system. Contain the impact by identifying every payment with no matching order, stop telling customers a payment succeeded until its outcome is known, and give support a holding message that is honest about the uncertainty. Then trace one affected payment end to end using its correlation ID, from the gateway request and response through the payment service state, the event published to the bus, and the callback delivery, to find where the outcome was lost.

Success is the order, not the gateway response.

BA Takeaway

Stop confirming success until the outcome is known. Find every payment with no matching order, give support an honest holding message, and trace one payment end to end by correlation ID to find where the outcome was lost.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Gateway request and response
→ Payment service state
→ Event published to the bus
→ Callback delivery

The real requirement isn't "Did the gateway answer?"

It's "What evidence proves the order system received the outcome?"

Have you ever been charged for an order the shop could not see?
takeaway: Trace one affected payment end to end using its correlation ID, from the gateway request and response through the payment service state, the event published to the bus, and the callback delivery.

title: Sent EUR 5,000, the employee received EUR 4,940
explain:
An ordering customer pays an employee EUR 5,000 with an MT103.
An intermediary bank deducts its charges on the way.
The employee receives EUR 4,940, and asks why EUR 60 is missing.
The ordering customer has no answer, because nobody explained the charge rule before the payment was sent.

Here's how that happens:

→ Ordering customer pays employee EUR 5,000 by MT103
→ Intermediary deducts EUR 60 in charges
→ Beneficiary bank credits EUR 4,940

The assumption was:
"The amount sent is the amount received."

The beneficiary bank credits the amount that arrives after the deductions, and the ordering customer must explain the difference to the employee. The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer rule matters before the payment is sent.

In a serial payment, every hand takes its charge.

BA Takeaway

Agree the charge-bearer rule before sending, and tell the beneficiary what will arrive. Under the serial method each intermediary deducts its charge, so the amount received is the amount sent minus every hand along the way.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Amount sent
→ Intermediary charges deducted
→ Amount credited to the beneficiary
→ Charge-bearer rule agreed up front

The real requirement isn't "How much did we send?"

It's "What evidence proves the beneficiary knows what will actually arrive?"

Have you ever had to explain to an employee why EUR 60 went missing between sending and receiving?
takeaway: The situation is a normal consequence of the serial method, and it is why the charge-bearer rule matters before the payment is sent.

title: Two legs, one payment, one thread: the UETR
explain:
A EUR 110,000 payment passes through a correspondent bank on its way abroad.
The correspondent sees two payments: the incoming payment from the sender, and the outgoing payment to the next bank.
Two legs, two messages, and the reconciliation team cannot prove they are the same payment.

Here's how that happens:

→ Correspondent receives the incoming payment
→ Correspondent sends the outgoing payment onward
→ UETR travels unchanged in both legs
→ UETR carried in field 121 of block 3
→ Bank reconciles incoming and outgoing legs

The assumption was:
"Each leg is a separate payment."

The two legs are linked by the unique end-to-end transaction reference, the UETR, which travels unchanged from one message to the next and is carried in field 121 of block 3. No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent.

The UETR is the thread. Break it and the payment cannot be reconciled.

BA Takeaway

Carry the UETR unchanged through every leg, in field 121 of block 3. No bank in the chain modifies it, because it is the only link between the payment received and the payment sent.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Incoming leg
→ Outgoing leg
→ UETR in field 121 of block 3
→ Reconciliation of both legs

The real requirement isn't "Did both legs settle?"

It's "What evidence proves the incoming and outgoing legs are the same payment?"

Have you ever tried to reconcile two legs of one payment and found the thread between them had been changed?
takeaway: No bank in the chain may modify field 121, because changing it would break the link that lets every bank reconcile the payment it received with the payment it sent.

title: The MT101 debited the customer. Where did the money sit?
explain:
A corporate customer sends an MT101 to pay its suppliers.
The debtor's account is debited at once.
But the suppliers are not paid yet, and the EUR 95,000 sits somewhere inside the bank, on an account nobody on the customer side can see.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT101 received from the customer
→ Debtor account debited to an intermediary account
→ MT103 generated to move the money onward
→ Funds debited from the intermediary account
→ Funds forwarded to the destination

The assumption was:
"The MT101 moves the money."

Accounting is done on the MT101 itself, in part: the debtor's account is debited and the funds are placed on an intermediary account inside the bank. When the MT103 is generated to move the money onward, the funds are debited from that intermediary account and forwarded to the destination. The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement.

The MT101 does the customer-side accounting. The MT103 does the interbank settlement.

BA Takeaway

Follow the money through the intermediary account. The MT101 debits the debtor and parks the funds inside the bank, and only the MT103 moves them onward to the destination.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Debtor account debit
→ Intermediary account inside the bank
→ MT103 generation
→ Interbank settlement

The real requirement isn't "Was the customer debited?"

It's "What evidence proves the funds moved from the intermediary account to the destination?"

Have you ever debited a customer on the MT101 and had to explain where the money sat before the MT103 went out?
takeaway: The MT101 therefore does the customer-side accounting, and the MT103 does the interbank settlement.

title: The MT103 has no town name. pacs.008 demands one.
explain:
An MT103 arrives for a EUR 45,000 payment, and it must be translated into pacs.008.
The MT103 carries no structured address.
pacs.008 requires a town name and a country code, and the town cannot be invented.
Guessing writes false data onto the payment. A blank fails validation. The payment is stuck between two message standards.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 taken in exactly as sent
→ Tested against every field pacs.008 requires
→ Town name missing, no source in the message
→ Enrichment needed from an authoritative source
→ Unresolvable gaps go to exception handling

The assumption was:
"Translate the message and fill the gaps."

MT to MX coexistence creates a data gap: an MT103 may carry no structured address, yet pacs.008 requires town name and country code. The missing town cannot be invented, guessing writes false data onto the payment and a blank fails validation. Handle the gap with explicit translation rules, enrichment from a trusted source, and exception governance for every field the old message cannot supply.

A missing town cannot be invented. Guessing writes false data onto a payment.

BA Takeaway

Write the translation rules before translating. Every field the old message cannot supply gets an enrichment rule from a trusted source, or a defined exception path, and guessing is never one of the options.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT103 as sent
→ pacs.008 requirements
→ Missing fields flagged
→ Enrichment from an authoritative source
→ Exception governance

The real requirement isn't "Can we translate it?"

It's "What evidence proves every required field came from a trusted source, not a guess?"

Have you ever had a payment stuck because the old message could not supply what the new one demands?

title: Two legs settled, two returns needed
explain:
A EUR 60,000 cover payment settles twice over: the pacs.008 instruction and the pacs.009 cover that moved funds between correspondents.
The customer payment is returned.
The team closes the case, and the nostro ledger still disagrees by EUR 60,000.

Here's how that happens:

→ pacs.008 instruction settles
→ pacs.009 cover settles between correspondents
→ Customer payment returned
→ Cover leg still open

The assumption was:
"Returning the customer payment unwinds the whole payment."

Returning the customer payment unwinds only the first leg; the cover needs its own pacs.004, matched to the original cover by UETR and settlement references. Both legs post to the Nostro ledger, so reconciliation must pair all four messages, instruction, cover, return of instruction, and return of cover.

One return unwinds one leg. A cover payment needs its own return.

BA Takeaway

Return both legs, and match each return to its original by UETR and settlement references. Reconciliation pairs all four messages, and the case closes only when the nostro ledger agrees.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Return of the instruction
→ Return of the cover
→ UETR matching
→ Nostro ledger pairing

The real requirement isn't "Was the customer refunded?"

It's "What evidence proves both legs were returned and the nostro ledger pairs all four messages?"

Have you ever returned the customer payment and forgotten the cover leg was still open?

title: EUR 5,000 debited, failed, and the books disagree
explain:
A 5,000 euro SEPA credit transfer debited the account.
It failed between the engine and clearing.
The customer is EUR 5,000 down, the books say the payment went, and reality says it never arrived.

Here's how that happens:

→ Account debited EUR 5,000
→ Payment failed between engine and clearing
→ Books and reality disagree

title: Acknowledged, then lost: the broker died before replication
explain:
A payment is charged once.
The retry charges it a second time.
Nothing alerted, because each component behaved exactly as designed, and the failure lived in the interaction between them.

Here's how that happens:

→ Leader acknowledges with acks=1
→ Broker dies before replication
→ Message lost, payment already charged
→ Retry charges a second time
→ No alert fires

The assumption was:
"An acknowledgement means the message is safe."

With acks=1 only the leader acknowledges, so a broker dying before replication loses the message, yet the payment had already been charged and the retry charged a second time. Nothing alerted because each component behaved as designed; the failure lived in the interaction. Fix the guarantees, acks=all with idempotent producers and dedup keys on every payment, add the transactional outbox pattern so the business record and the event cannot diverge, and keep reconciliation as the backstop.

→ Acknowledgement guarantee
→ Idempotent producers and dedup keys
→ Transactional outbox
→ Reconciliation as backstop

The real requirement isn't "Did each component work?"

title: Processed, timed out, then paid twice
explain:
A core banking API processes a EUR 35,000 transaction.
Then it times out before responding.
The caller, believing it failed, re-submits a completed transaction, and the customer is debited twice.

Here's how that happens:

→ API processes the transaction
→ Timeout before the response arrives
→ Caller retry re-submits the completed transaction
→ Customer debited twice

The assumption was:
"A timeout means it did not happen."

The missing controls were idempotency keys, a smart timeout strategy, and a reconciliation layer. The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first, asking what actually happened to the money.

On any timeout, ask what actually happened to the money.

BA Takeaway

Put idempotency keys on every mutating call, keep a pending-state model that checks state before acting, and make it a standing rule: on any timeout, query the true state first, never blindly re-submit.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Idempotency keys on every call
→ Pending-state transaction model
→ Smart timeout strategy
→ Reconciliation layer

The real requirement isn't "Did the call time out?"

It's "What evidence proves whether the transaction completed before the timeout?"

Have you ever re-submitted a transaction after a timeout and paid it twice?
takeaway: The fix is idempotency keys on every mutating call, a pending-state transaction model that checks state before acting, and a standing rule that on any timeout the true state is queried first.
